name: John Singer Sargent
summary: Florence-born American painter who made London his base and became the pre-eminent society portraitist of the Edwardian age. In later life he turned increasingly to watercolour and to mural schemes, but it is his portraits that defined an era's image of itself.
grave: An upright Portland stone grave-marker modelled on an Attic stele, which also commemorates his sister Emily. The foot reads 'HE GIVETH HIS BELOVED SLEEP'; the motto at the top is recorded differently by the cemetery ('LABORARE EST ORARE') and by the Historic England listing ('LABORARE EST HONORARE').
notes: Plot number disputed: the Brookwood Cemetery Society (and Wikipedia, citing it) gives Plot 35, 'the Ring', but the cemetery's own listed-monuments page gives Plot 27. Inscription wording also differs between sources (see grave). Wikipedia gives his death as 14 April 1925 in the text but 15 April in its infobox; 14 April is used here.

name: Dame Rebecca West
summary: Born Cicily Isabel Fairfield, she took her pen-name from an Ibsen heroine and became one of the most formidable novelists, critics and reporters of the twentieth century. Her work ranged from suffrage journalism to her monumental Yugoslav travelogue Black Lamb and Grey Falcon and her reports on the Nuremberg trials.
grave: A simple headstone that records her three names, according to the Brookwood Cemetery Society.
notes: Plot 81 is given by both the Brookwood Cemetery Society and the cemetery. Her birth name is spelt differently: the cemetery gives Cicily Fairfield, the Society Cicily Isabel Fairfield, and Wikipedia Cecily Isabel Fairfield. She was made CBE in 1949 and DBE in 1959.

name: Dennis Wheatley
summary: Best-selling author of thrillers and occult novels, above all The Devil Rides Out, whose books sold in vast numbers from the 1930s to the 1960s. During the Second World War he worked with the London Controlling Section and the Joint Planning Staff of the War Cabinet on strategic deception and planning.
grave: His ashes are interred in the Glades of Remembrance at Brookwood following cremation at Tooting; no description of the memorial was found.
notes: He is also commemorated on the Baker/Yates family monument at West Norwood Cemetery (grave 26,071, square 50, according to John Clarke); the cemetery's own page misspells the family as 'Baker/Yeats'. Wikipedia places the ashes in the 'South Cemetery section ... under a tall tree near the entrance'; the cemetery and John Clarke say Glades of Remembrance. No plot number found.

name: William De Morgan
summary: Potter and designer, a friend of William Morris, whose lustreware and tiles are among the finest achievements of the Arts and Crafts movement. Late in life he reinvented himself as a best-selling novelist.
grave: A tall neo-Grec Carrara marble stele shared with his wife Evelyn; the relief, designed by Evelyn, shows an angel with outstretched arms pleading with a female figure of Death, with an inverted torch, who turns her back, beneath an eared pediment with a pair of hearts. The inscription describes him as 'Artist - Potter - Inventor - Novelist'.
notes: The listing and the cemetery give the epitaph as 'Sorrow is only of the earth'; Wikipedia's article on Evelyn De Morgan gives 'Sorrow is only of the flesh' and says the relief was carved by Sir George Frampton, an attribution the listing calls 'perhaps open to question'.

name: Evelyn De Morgan
summary: Born Evelyn Pickering, she was one of the most accomplished painters of the later Pre-Raphaelite circle, producing richly coloured allegorical and Symbolist canvases. She died two years after her husband William and was buried in the same grave.
grave: She designed the relief on the couple's Carrara marble stele herself: an angel with outstretched arms pleading with a female figure of Death, with an inverted torch, who turns her back.
notes: Shares the grave of William De Morgan (d. 1917). The listing and the cemetery give the epitaph as 'Sorrow is only of the earth'; Wikipedia gives 'of the flesh' and says the relief was carved by Sir George Frampton, an attribution the listing calls 'perhaps open to question'.

name: Sir Luke Fildes
summary: Sir Samuel Luke Fildes began as a social-realist illustrator and painter of the London poor and became one of the most popular painters of his day, later painting Edwardian state portraits. His painting The Doctor (1891) became one of the best-loved images of Victorian art.
grave: A Portland stone headstone in the form of an Athenian stele, with an elaborate palmette and acanthus-enriched head; his wife Fanny is also commemorated. It is listed as a late example of a Neo-classical memorial.
notes: Birth year varies: Wikipedia gives 3 October 1843; the listing and the cemetery give 1844 (RA, 1844-1927); The Times obituary gave 3 October 1844 'or according to some 1843'. Death date: The Times death notice gives 27 February 1927 (at 11 Melbury Road, Kensington), Wikipedia 28 February; 27 February is used here.

name: Henri van Laun
summary: Writer, teacher and translator who did much to bring French literature to English readers, translating Molière, Lesage and La Bruyère and Hippolyte Taine's History of English Literature. He was a friend of Taine.
grave: An unusual terracotta monument by the sculptor Emmeline Halse: a white-glazed oval portrait relief set against books and scrolls on a square plinth with griffin monopods at the corners. Garlands on the sides of the plinth carry the names of Molière, Lesage, Taine and La Bruyère, and the rear bears the inscription 'Erected to the memory of my father'.
notes: Birth year given as 1819 by Historic England and the cemetery, 1820 by Wikipedia. Wikipedia (citing the Dictionary of National Biography and The Times obituary) calls him Dutch-born and gives his death as 19 January 1896; the listing and the cemetery call him a Belgian writer and critic. The cemetery suggests a link to the terracotta works at nearby Compton.

name: Arthur Melville
summary: Scottish painter whose broad, vivid watercolours of Eastern life and of Venice, painted after travels in Persia, Egypt and Turkey, influenced the Glasgow Boys. He died of typhoid fever at Witley, Surrey, in 1904.
grave: His ashes were first buried in the garden of his home at Witley; on 10 July 1909 his widow had them reburied on Brookwood Heath, just beyond the cemetery's formal boundary, under a pink granite kerb and upright block erected by the London Necropolis Company. The block was smashed in the 1970s and discarded; stonemasons repaired it in 2022 for the Brookwood Cemetery Society and it was re-dedicated in September 2023.
area: Brookwood Heath, just outside the cemetery boundary
notes: Strictly the grave lies outside the cemetery, on Brookwood Heath (an SSSI). The Society's own papers differ on small points: the original stone is inscribed 'born 10th April 1858 (sic), died 29th August 1904', while the Society's 2023 programme gives 10 April 1855 to 28 August 1904, as Wikipedia does. The Society's 2022 letter dates the reburial 10 July 1909 (as Wikipedia does); the 2023 programme says the stone was set up on 10 July 1908. Wikipedia dates the restoration to 2023; the Society's pages show the repair completed in November 2022 and the re-dedication in September 2023 (the programme file is dated 24-9-2023).

name: Dame Zaha Hadid
summary: Baghdad-born British architect whose fluid, curving buildings, from the London Aquatics Centre to the MAXXI in Rome, made her one of the most celebrated designers of her time. In 2004 she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize.
grave: She lies between her father, Mohammed Hadid, and her brother, Foulath Hadid; she designed her father's memorial.
notes: She died in Miami (Wikipedia: at Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she was being treated for bronchitis). The Society's newsletter says she was buried at Brookwood after a service at London's Grand Mosque. No numbered plot is given in the sources read.

name: Naji al-Ali
summary: Palestinian political cartoonist, creator of Handala, the barefoot refugee child seen from behind who became a symbol of Palestinian identity. He was shot outside the London offices of the Kuwaiti newspaper al-Qabas on 22 July 1987 and died five weeks later without regaining consciousness; the killing remains unsolved.
grave: Buried in the Muslim ground at Brookwood; no description of the memorial could be verified.
notes: Wikipedia says his will asked to be buried beside his father at Ain al-Hilweh in Lebanon, which proved impossible to arrange, and that he was buried in the 'Brookwood Islamic Cemetery' (the Muslim ground at Brookwood). Birth year is uncertain: Wikipedia gives c. 1938, its list of Brookwood burials 1937?. In August 2017 detectives relaunched the investigation into the murder, thirty years after his death. Neither the cemetery nor the Brookwood Cemetery Society has a page on him that I could find.

name: Douglas Freshfield
summary: Barrister, mountaineer and travel writer, editor of the Alpine Journal and later president of both the Alpine Club and the Royal Geographical Society, whose explorations extended to the Caucasus and the Himalaya.
grave: Buried in front of the memorial to their son Henry Douglas Freshfield (1877-1891), on which he and his wife Augusta (d. 1911) are also commemorated. It was sculpted by Edward Onslow Ford in 1892 in Carrara and Siena marble with bronze enrichment and wrought-iron railings, and the cemetery calls it one of the most lavish in Brookwood.
notes: Wikipedia, citing John Clarke's London's Necropolis (p. 173), says he is buried in front of his son's memorial; the cemetery and the listing say the memorial is also to his parents, 'Augusta (d.1911) and Douglas (d.1934)'. He died at Wych Cross Place, Forest Row, Sussex.

name: Dr Robert Knox
summary: Distinguished Edinburgh anatomy lecturer whose career was ruined after 1828, when Burke and Hare, who had supplied bodies to his anatomy school, were found to have murdered their victims; he was not summonsed to give evidence, but was popularly held to be as guilty as they. He ended his days in London as a pathological anatomist, dying in Hackney.
grave: Buried in Plot 100; a small granite block on the grave was placed there in 1966 by the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh.
notes: The Society's page says the small granite block was placed 'as recently as 1966'. Wikipedia says he died at 9 Lambe Terrace, Hackney, and was pathological anatomist to the Free Cancer Hospital (the Society calls it the Royal Marsden Cancer Hospital at Brompton). Earlier claims about a ledger stone, its wording and its rediscovery by Professor Eric Mekie could not be verified and have been removed.

name: Daniel Solander
summary: Swedish botanist and pupil of Linnaeus who sailed with Joseph Banks on Cook's first voyage in HMS Endeavour, helping to collect and describe the plants of the expedition. He died at Banks's London home in Soho Square.
grave: Reburied in the Swedish burial ground (Swedish Church ground) at Brookwood, where an 'impressive monument' was erected by the Swedish Royal Society in 1913; no fuller description was found.
notes: Originally buried at the Swedish Church on Princes Square in London; burials there ended in 1856 when the Privy Council withdrew permission, and Solander was among those exhumed from the church yard and reburied at Brookwood. The date of his reburial was not found; the monument dates from 1913. Wikipedia places him in the 'Swedish Section'.

name: Sir Arthur Schuster
summary: German-born British mathematical physicist whose work spanned spectroscopy, electrochemistry, optics, X-radiography and the application of harmonic analysis to physics. He was knighted in 1920.
grave: No description found.
notes: The cemetery's page gives only his birth year (1851) and his death date; the day of birth, 12 September 1851, is from Wikipedia. He died at Hare Hatch, according to Wikipedia.

name: Charles Bradlaugh
summary: Radical, republican and atheist, founder of the National Secular Society, he was elected MP for Northampton in 1880 but kept out of the Commons for years after asking to affirm rather than swear the religious oath, and was first allowed to take his seat in January 1886 as the first atheist to become an MP. His long fight led to the Oaths Act of 1888, which legalised affirmation.
grave: A large family grave in the North Cemetery. The memorial of about 1892-93, in pink granite, bronze and cast iron, carried a bronze bust by the sculptor Francis Verheyden, placed in 1893; the bust was removed in 1938 and never traced, and a bronze wreath was also lost. An authentic replica bust and wreath were unveiled on 17 October 2021, with the support of the National Secular Society, the Brookwood Cemetery Society and the cemetery.
notes: John Clarke dates the bust's removal to the night of 12-13 September 1938, the eve of an international freethinkers' congress; the cemetery says only that it was stolen 'some years ago'. His funeral on 3 February 1891 drew great crowds: Clarke says over 5,000 people jammed the approach roads to Waterloo and three special trains were run, while Wikipedia says 3,000 mourners attended, including the young Gandhi. The grave is described as off Holly Avenue.

name: Shapurji Saklatvala
summary: Bombay-born Parsi who was Communist MP for Battersea North in 1922-23 and again from 1924 to 1929, among the first people of Indian heritage elected to the House of Commons, and an outspoken opponent of British imperialism. His mother was a sister of J. N. Tata.
grave: He was cremated at Golders Green and his remains were buried on 21 January 1936 in his mother's tomb in the Parsi burial ground at Brookwood, according to Wikipedia; no cemetery or Society description was found.
notes: The burial rests on Wikipedia alone: no page of the cemetery, the Society, John Clarke or Exploring Surrey's Past that I could read mentions him. The earlier remarks that another account places him beside both parents near J. N. Tata, and that the Zoroastrian association admitted his children but not his non-Parsi wife, came from pages I could not open and have been removed.

name: Sir Mancherjee Bhownaggree
summary: Bombay Parsi lawyer who sat as Conservative MP for Bethnal Green North East from 1895 to 1906, the second Indian after Dadabhai Naoroji to enter the House of Commons.
grave: Buried in the Parsi section. His gravestone is inscribed 'Sir Mancherjee Merwanjee Bhownaggree K.C.I.E. Born Bombay 27th August 1851 (Nadmi Nowroze) Died London 14th November 1933'.
notes: Wikipedia gives his birth date as 15 August 1851; the gravestone, as transcribed by Exploring Surrey's Past, reads 27th August 1851 with the Parsi calendar note 'Nadmi Nowroze', so only the year is used here. Wikipedia counts him the third British MP of Indian descent, after David Ochterlony Dyce Sombre and Naoroji.
calling: MP for Bethnal Green North East

name: Lord Edward Pelham-Clinton
summary: Second son of the 5th Duke of Newcastle, briefly Liberal MP for North Nottinghamshire (1865–68), and later Groom-in-Waiting and then Master of the Household to Queen Victoria from 1894 until her death in 1901.
grave: An exceptional Neo-Baroque bronze group on a Portland stone base, commemorating him and his wife Matilda (d. 1892): a recumbent, semi-draped woman, a kneeling weeping mourner and an angel with outstretched wings hovering above. The sculptor is unknown and the inscription panels have been lost.
notes: Often styled Lord Edward Clinton. He lived nearby, at The Heights, Witley. The listing suggests the work recalls that of Princess Louise, but says this needs more research before any attribution.
calling: Master of the Household to Queen Victoria

name: John Lynch
summary: Cork Fenian, a widower and former publican, convicted of treason felony in December 1865 on an informer's word and sentenced to ten years' penal servitude; he died in Woking Prison in 1866.
grave: Buried on 6 June 1866 in the Roman Catholic pauper section; the grave's exact position is unknown but lies somewhere in the woodland beyond plot 134. A stone plaque placed by the National Graves Association of Ireland in 2004 on the wall of the former Catholic chapel (plot 124) commemorates him.
notes: Grave location unknown. The cemetery gives 2 June 1866 as the date of death and 6 June as the burial date; John Clarke's 2002 article says he died on 6 June 1866 and was buried in the Catholic pauper ground. His only other memorials are on the National Monument in Cork and a plaque in Devonshire Street, Cork.

name: St Edward the Martyr
summary: Anglo-Saxon King of England, murdered at Corfe in 978 and soon venerated as a saint. Relics identified as his were found at Shaftesbury Abbey in 1931 and, after years of negotiation, given to the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia, which received and enshrined them at Brookwood on 15 and 16 September 1984.
grave: The relics rest in the church of St Edward the Martyr, served by the St Edward Brotherhood, an Orthodox community within the cemetery.
notes: The Brookwood Cemetery Society gives his dates as c. 959-978/9; Wikipedia (citing the ODNB) gives c. 962-18 March 978, and John Clarke says the year of the murder, 978 or 979, is uncertain. The finder, John Wilson-Claridge (1905-1993), donated the relics. Ownership was contested: a High Court summons arrived days before the 1984 enshrinement, the court allowed the relics to be received and enshrined but required them to go back to a bank vault until security was arranged, the Attorney General at first claimed they belonged to the Queen, and by an Order dated 31 March 1995 the Chancery Division dismissed the case (John Clarke). Wikipedia dates a High Court ruling in favour of Brookwood to 1988 and says historians are very sceptical that the bones are Edward's.

name: Dr Gottlieb Wilhelm Leitner
summary: Pest-born orientalist, linguist and educationist who worked in Lahore before founding the Oriental Institute at Woking, where the Shah Jahan Mosque, Britain's first purpose-built mosque, was built in 1889. In 1884 he had a plot at Brookwood set aside that became Britain's first Muslim burial ground.
grave: A Carrara marble bust within a curved niche and pink granite surround, inscribed 'THE LEARNED ARE HONOURED IN THEIR WORK'; the memorial also records his birth at Budapest and death at Bonn, and his wife Lina Olympia (d. 1912).
notes: He died in Bonn. The cemetery lists him as 'Plot 2, South Cemetery'; he lies in the main cemetery, not in the Muslim ground he had set aside. His name is given as 'Gottlieb Wilhelm' (Wikipedia), 'Gottlieb William' (the memorial and listing) and 'Gottleib' (the cemetery's page title). The Society dates the Oriental Institute to 1884; Exploring Surrey's Past also gives 1881.

name: Lord Headley (Rowland Allanson-Winn, 5th Baron Headley)
summary: Irish peer who converted to Islam in 1913, taking the name Shaikh Rahmatullah al-Farooq, and became a leading member of the Woking Muslim Mission; he founded the British Muslim Society in 1914. He is reported to have been offered, and declined, the throne of Albania in 1925.
grave: Buried in the Muslim ground at Brookwood; no description of the memorial could be verified.
notes: Wikipedia gives Codford, Wiltshire, as his place of death; he twice performed the Hajj, according to Wikipedia. John Clarke lists him among the late Victorian converts buried in the Muslim cemetery and calls him a co-founder of the Woking Muslim Mission. Earlier claims that he lies a few yards from Pickthall and Abdullah Yusuf Ali, and that BACSA calls him the first peer to perform the Hajj, came from pages I could not open and have been removed.

name: Marmaduke Pickthall
summary: Novelist and journalist who declared his conversion to Islam in November 1917 and published The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930), one of the most widely known and used English translations of the Qur'an.
grave: Buried in the Muslim section, the old 'Muhammadan' burial ground; Wikipedia's photograph caption says the grave is inscribed with Qur'an 2:112 in his own translation.
notes: Died at the Porthminster Hotel, St Ives, Cornwall. Born at Cambridge Terrace, near Regent's Park, London (Wikipedia). The cemetery lists him under 'Muhammadan Plot' and gives no plot number.

name: Abdullah Yusuf Ali
summary: Indian-born barrister, civil servant and scholar whose English translation and commentary of the Qur'an, first published in 1934, remains one of the most widely known. He died alone in a London hospital in 1953 after a heart attack at a London County Council home for the elderly.
grave: Buried in the Muslim section at Brookwood; his funeral and burial were arranged by the Pakistan High Commission. Wikipedia says Pickthall was buried there before him.
notes: Birth date given as 14 April (Wikipedia, citing the Oxford DNB) or 4 April 1872 (John Clarke). He suffered his heart attack on 10 December 1953 in an LCC home for the elderly in Dovehouse Street, Chelsea, and died the same day at St Stephen's Hospital, Fulham.

name: Abdullah Quilliam
summary: Liverpool solicitor William Henry Quilliam converted to Islam and founded the Liverpool Muslim Institute, which housed Britain's first functioning mosque, opened in 1889. He later left Liverpool and lived for years under the name Henri Marcel Leon (also given as Haroun Mustapha Leon).
grave: An unmarked grave in the Muslim section; Wikipedia says Abdullah Yusuf Ali and Marmaduke Pickthall were later buried near him.
notes: The cemetery's page is headed 'Muhammadan Plot' and 'Unmarked Grave'. Wikipedia places his grave, and those of Yusuf Ali, Pickthall and Lord Headley, in the 'M1 Muslim Section'. He died at Taviton Street, Bloomsbury, London.
calling: Solicitor; founder of the Liverpool Muslim Institute

name: Ross Lowis Mangles
summary: Bengal civil servant who joined the force sent to relieve Arrah in 1857; when it was ambushed, he carried a wounded soldier of the 37th Regiment for several miles during the retreat on 30 July, despite being wounded himself. He is one of only five civilians to be awarded the Victoria Cross, presented by Queen Victoria at Windsor on 4 January 1860.
grave: A cross memorial with inscription panels inside a decorative cast-iron surround. In May 2006 the Brookwood Cemetery Society had the cross reset upright, cleaned the inscription panels, and cleaned and repainted the surround.
area: South cemetery, facing St George's Avenue
notes: The cemetery, John Clarke and Wikipedia all call him one of only five civilians awarded the VC. He died at his home in Pirbright. Plot 31 also holds the Drake family mausoleum.

name: John Sherwood-Kelly
summary: South African-born officer who won the Victoria Cross at Marcoing on 20 November 1917, during the Battle of Cambrai, while commanding the 1st Battalion, Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers. His medal is in the National Museum of Military History in Johannesburg.
grave: Given a full military funeral; Wikipedia gives the inscription on his gravestone as 'One who never turned his back but marches breast forward'.
notes: The cemetery and John Clarke both give Plot 81. Birthplace is given as Queenstown (the cemetery and Wikipedia's text) or Lady Frere (Wikipedia's infobox), Cape Colony. He died in a Kensington nursing home after complications from malaria (cemetery).

name: Rev. William Addison
summary: Anglican army chaplain awarded the Victoria Cross for carrying a wounded man to cover and tending others under heavy fire at Sannaiyat, Mesopotamia, on 9 April 1916. He remained an army chaplain after the war, serving in Malta, Khartoum and Shanghai, and was rector of Coltishall with Great Hautbois in Norfolk from 1938 to 1958.
grave: A cross memorial with inscription panels. By 2007 it was badly weathered, with the foundations of the cross exposed and the inscription largely illegible; in autumn 2007 the Brookwood Cemetery Society had the stonework cleaned and repaired, the panels made legible and the foundations made sound.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives his birth as 16 September 1883 but its text and lead give 18 September 1883, at North Warnborough, Hampshire; government authorities long believed he was born in Kent until the error was found, and the cemetery says he 'came from Odiham, Hants'. The VC action was on 9 April 1916 (cemetery, John Clarke, Wikipedia). He died at St Leonards-on-Sea on 7 January 1962; his funeral at St Barnabas's Church, Bexhill-on-Sea, and the burial at Brookwood were both on 11 January.

name: William Reynolds
summary: Private in the Scots Fusilier Guards awarded the Victoria Cross for rallying men round the Colours at the Battle of the Alma on 20 September 1854; he received it from Queen Victoria at the first VC investiture, in Hyde Park on 26 June 1857. He is the only Crimean War VC on John Clarke's list of holders at Brookwood.
grave: Buried in a '2nd class grave' after dying in the workhouse dispensary of the Strand Union; the Scots Guards Association Club placed a memorial there on 27 April 2007.
notes: The cemetery's text, John Clarke's biography and Wikipedia give his death as 20 October 1869 (aged 42, in the workhouse dispensary of the Strand Union, central London); the headings of the cemetery's page and of John Clarke's VC list read 1827-1867. He had worked as a bank messenger.

name: Carroll Gibbons
summary: American-born pianist, bandleader and composer who made his career in Britain. He led the Savoy Hotel Orpheans, jointly from 1931 and alone from June 1932, and was the hotel's Director of Entertainments from 1950 until his death in 1954.
grave: Buried near the chapel in Plot 124; no description of the memorial found.
area: North cemetery, near the cemetery chapel (Roman Catholic grounds)
notes: The cemetery's page heads his name 'Carol Gibbons'. Wikipedia gives his birth name as Charles Richard Gibbons, born in Clinton, Massachusetts; he died at the London Clinic of a coronary thrombosis.

name: Sir Thomas Beecham
summary: Conductor and impresario, founder with Malcolm Sargent of the London Philharmonic (1932) and later of the Royal Philharmonic (1946), and an advocate of the music of Delius.
grave: No longer at Brookwood: buried here on 10 March 1961, two days after his death, but exhumed in 1991 and reburied in St Peter's churchyard, Limpsfield, Surrey, close to the joint grave of Delius and his wife Jelka.
notes: Former burial only. Wikipedia gives 'changes at Brookwood' as the reason for the move and cites John Lucas, Thomas Beecham: An Obsession with Music (2008), p. 339; I found no mention of him in the cemetery's own pages or in John Clarke's, so the burial and the removal rest on Wikipedia and that book.

name: Christopher Hewett
summary: English actor and theatre director who worked on Broadway and in American television, best known for the title role of the English butler in the sitcom Mr. Belvedere (1985-90).
grave: Wikipedia gives Brookwood Cemetery as his resting place; he died at his home in Los Angeles. No cemetery record, plot or description of the grave was found.
notes: The Brookwood burial is stated in Wikipedia's infobox and in its Brookwood articles; the cemetery's own pages do not mention him. His memorial service was held at St Victor's Church, West Hollywood, on 10 August 2001. Wikipedia cites the FreeBMD index for his birth on 5 April 1922; its Brookwood Cemetery article gives his dates as 1921-2001.

name: Edith Thompson
summary: Convicted with her lover Frederick Bywaters of the murder of her husband Percy, and hanged at Holloway on 9 January 1923, the same morning Bywaters was hanged at Pentonville; the case against her rested largely on her love letters. Her execution became a cause célèbre.
grave: Reburied at Brookwood in 1971 with Styllou Christofi, Amelia Sach and Annie Walters in a single grave in Plot 117, unmarked until a grey granite memorial to the four women was dedicated on 13 November 1993. Wikipedia gives her epitaph as 'Sleep on beloved. Her death was a legal formality'. Her remains were exhumed on 20 November 2018 and reburied at the City of London Cemetery on 22 November.
notes: Remains moved twice. Holloway's burial ground was cleared when the prison was rebuilt in 1971 and the bodies taken to Brookwood; René Weis wrote in 1988 that her family had not been told. She was exhumed from Brookwood on 20 November 2018 and reburied on 22 November in her parents' grave at the City of London Cemetery (cemetery and John Clarke; Wikipedia dates the exhumation 22 November and the burial two days later). She is therefore no longer at Brookwood. The cemetery says the memorial was placed in October 1993; the service of dedication was on 13 November.

name: Margaret, Duchess of Argyll
summary: Born Margaret Whigham, she was presented at court in 1930 and known as the debutante of that year, and remained associated with glamour and elegance. Her much-publicised 1963 divorce from the 11th Duke of Argyll turned on Polaroid photographs of her with an unidentified man.
grave: Buried in Plot 119 beside her first husband, Charles Sweeny, who had died in March 1993; they share a grave. No description of the memorial was found.
notes: Plot 119 is given by the cemetery's own page and by Wikipedia's article on Charles Sweeny. Her requiem mass was held at the Church of the Immaculate Conception, Farm Street, Mayfair. She died in a nursing home in Pimlico, London, after a fall.

name: Sir Cosmo Duff Gordon
summary: Scottish landowner, baronet and fencer who survived the sinking of the Titanic in 1912 in Lifeboat No. 1, which held only 12 people against a capacity of 40. Allegations that he had bribed its crew not to row back for survivors brought him press criticism, although the British inquiry called the charge unfounded.
grave: He and his wife Lucy lie together in Plot 25; the Brookwood Cemetery Society shows a joint memorial to them, but no description of it was found.
notes: Plot 25 is given by both the cemetery and the Brookwood Cemetery Society. He and Lucy travelled on the Titanic as 'Mr and Mrs Morgan'. The cemetery says he represented Britain at the 1908 Olympic Games; Wikipedia says he won a team épée silver at the 1906 Intercalated Games and served on the organising committee of the 1908 Olympics.

name: Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon ('Lucile')
summary: Leading couturier who founded the fashion house Lucile, with branches in London, Paris, New York and Chicago, and pioneered the staged fashion parade with professional mannequins. She survived the Titanic with her husband Sir Cosmo.
grave: Buried with her husband in Plot 25.
notes: She died of breast cancer complicated by pneumonia in a Putney nursing home on 20 April 1935, exactly four years after her husband, from whom she had been estranged since 1915 (Wikipedia). The Brookwood Cemetery Society gives Plot 25.

name: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata
summary: Founder of the Tata Group, India's largest conglomerate, who set himself four goals: an iron and steel company, a world-class learning institution, a hotel and a hydroelectric plant. He died at Bad Nauheim in Germany.
grave: One of the three Tata family mausolea beside the entrance to the Parsi burial ground; his stands between those of his sons Dorabji and Ratanji.
notes: Wikipedia says he was buried in the Parsi burial ground at Brookwood. The Tata mausolea are not among the 15 listed monuments named on the cemetery's listed-monuments page.

name: Sir Ratanji Tata
summary: Younger son of Jamsetji Tata, industrialist and philanthropist. He died at St Ives, Cornwall, and was buried at Brookwood beside his father.
grave: One of the three Tata family mausolea beside the entrance to the Parsi burial ground.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives his death as 5 September 1918 and its text as 6 September.

name: Sir Dorabji Tata
summary: Elder son of Jamsetji Tata and second chairman of the Tata group (1904-32), who was closely involved in his father's plans for iron and steel and hydroelectric power. He was knighted in 1910.
grave: One of the three Tata family mausolea beside the entrance to the Parsi burial ground; Wikipedia says he is buried there alongside his wife Meherbai.
notes: He died at Bad Kissingen, Germany.

name: Sir Ernest William Moir
summary: Civil engineer who worked on the Forth Bridge, the Blackwall Tunnel and the Hudson River tunnel in New York, where he invented an airlock chamber to treat decompression (compressed-air) sickness.
grave: A Grade II listed family monument by the sculptor Lilian Wade: a bronze figure of Peace holding an olive branch on a stylised Ionic column bearing a relief profile portrait within a laurel wreath, on a pink granite base, set in an evergreen glade. It is a memorial to Lieutenant Rex Moir, who died in 1915, and also commemorates his parents; Wikipedia says Sir Ernest is buried in the family plot beneath it.
notes: First listed 23 July 2004. Historic England's text says Rex Moir was killed in 1915 (the cemetery's copy says died); Wikipedia says he died of meningitis in London.

name: Douglas Vickers
summary: Sheffield industrialist, chairman of the armaments firm Vickers from 1918 to 1926, and Conservative MP for Sheffield Hallam from 1918 to 1922.
grave: A pair of Portland stone memorials within a stone kerb: his own, of 1937, is a rectangular chest tomb in the style of Sir Edwin Lutyens with a heraldic cartouche at each end, beside the c. 1928 memorial to Oliver Vickers, an early Royal Flying Corps ace, which bears an eagle and the RAF motto Per ardua ad astra.
area: South cemetery (former Anglican section), facing St George's Avenue
listed: Grade II, list entry 1391035 (Vickers family grave)
notes: First listed 23 July 2004. The list text says Oliver Vickers's father founded the Vickers aviation company; Wikipedia names Oliver Henry Douglas Vickers (1898-1928) as a son of Douglas Vickers.

name: Dugald Drummond
summary: Scottish locomotive engineer who became locomotive superintendent of the North British Railway in 1875, moved to the Caledonian Railway in 1882, and in 1895 became locomotive engineer of the London and South Western Railway (Chief Mechanical Engineer from 1905).
grave: A family grave in Plot 38, just a stone's throw from the former terminus of the London Necropolis Railway; the cemetery lies beside the LSWR main line.
notes: He died at his home in Surbiton. Wikipedia, following C. Hamilton Ellis, says he was scalded by the water of a hot mustard bath, neglected the burns and died after gangrene and amputation; the popular story of a scalding on the footplate is described as a myth.

name: Ramadan Güney
summary: Paphos-born Turkish Cypriot businessman who helped found London's first Turkish Cypriot mosque and, as chairman of the UK Turkish Islamic Trust, which wanted burial facilities for its members, bought Brookwood Cemetery in 1985.
grave: Buried in his family vault at Brookwood on the evening of Friday 10 November 2006, after a service at his mosque in London; no description of the monument was found.
notes: The cemetery's page is headed 'Plot M3'. He died in Cyprus (John Clarke: of a heart attack; Wikipedia: in North Cyprus). Wikipedia reports that in 2011 the inheritance of the cemetery was successfully challenged.

name: Dodi Fayed
summary: Egyptian film producer and eldest child of Mohamed Al-Fayed, killed in the Paris car crash that also killed Diana, Princess of Wales. He was buried at Brookwood shortly after his death.
grave: No longer at Brookwood: buried temporarily in Plot 1, where his body rested for 40 days before it was moved to Oxted; Wikipedia says he was re-interred in October 1997 on the grounds of Barrow Green Court, the Fayed family estate at Oxted, Surrey.
notes: Temporary burial only. John Clarke records that the grave attracted enormous numbers of visitors. Most sources, and his gravestone, give his birth as 15 April 1955; since 2022 some sources have given 17 April (Wikipedia).
